In the third-floor pantry of the call centre, Harsha had the phone on speaker without realising. 'Sir, to reverse the fraud, share the six-digit code now,' the caller said. He had already sent 2,000 that afternoon as a 'security deposit'.
Gargi, rinsing her cup, turned round and mouthed, 'Hang up.'
He did. His hands were cold.
'Open your bank app. The real one,' Gargi said. The app showed the 2,000 debit and nothing about any fraud case. Harsha rang the number printed on his debit card, asked them to block the card and flag the transfer, then dialled the cybercrime helpline while Gargi wrote the times and amounts on a napkin.
'I feel so stupid,' he muttered between calls.
'You stopped it at 2,000,' Gargi said. 'That's the part that counts.'

qa.q: What did the caller ask Harsha to share?
qa.a: The caller asked Harsha to share the six-digit code.

qa.q: What does Harsha feel even after hanging up, and how can you tell?
qa.a: His hands are cold and he mutters that he feels stupid, showing fear mixed with embarrassment.

qa.q: Which of Harsha's steps gave him the best chance to limit harm?
qa.a: Hanging up, checking the real bank app, calling the number on his card to block it and flag the transfer, and reporting quickly to the cybercrime helpline with the times and amounts written down.

qa.q: How does Gargi see what happened?
qa.a: Gargi sees it as a scam Harsha stopped early, not as foolishness, which is why she says stopping at 2,000 is what counts.

grounding: It shows a victim hanging up, checking through the official app and card number, involving a trusted colleague and reporting fast to the bank and cybercrime helpline.

Subject: You were right about 'safe accounts'

Hi Thomas,
Weird week. On Tuesday someone rang saying they were from my bank's fraud team. They knew my name and the last four digits of my card. They said my account was compromised, that I had to move my savings to a 'safe account' before midnight, and not to tell anyone because 'the fraudster might be close to you'.
I'd moved £300 before something snagged. You once told me banks never ask you to move money.
So I hung up mid-sentence, opened the bank's own app and called from there. They froze the transfer and said calling within the hour really helped. Then I rang the fraud reporting line and told my flatmate, who made me toast and sat with me.
Still shaky, but mostly okay. Thank you for that random lecture last year.
Noor

qa.q: How much had Noor moved before stopping?
qa.a: Noor had moved £300 before something snagged.

qa.q: Why is Noor writing to Thomas in particular?
qa.a: Noor feels grateful, because Thomas's old warning that banks never ask you to move money is what made something snag during the call.

qa.q: What did Noor's quick steps achieve?
qa.a: Hanging up and calling through the bank's own app within the hour let the bank freeze the transfer, and telling the flatmate meant Noor wasn't alone with it.

qa.q: What might Thomas feel reading this email?
qa.a: Thomas will probably feel relieved that Noor is safe and glad the random lecture mattered, perhaps with a pang at how close it was.

grounding: It shows a victim cutting off a caller, checking through the bank's own app, reporting within the hour and telling a trusted person.

passage:
Jatin, you asked what I'd do differently. Nothing about the end. The end I got right.
It was a courier call, the usual: a parcel in my name, drugs inside, "stay on the line, don't tell anyone, pay to clear your name". I had already typed the amount into the app. Then something in me just said: stop.
I hung up. Mid-sentence. My hands were shaking so much I dropped the phone. Then I did four things. I called the courier company on the number from its official website: no such parcel. I called my sister and told her everything, even the embarrassing parts. I called my bank and blocked online transfers. And I reported the number to the cyber-crime helpline within the hour.
Didn't lose a rupee. But if I'd waited to think it over till morning, they'd have called back and I'd have paid. Speed is everything. That's the Suraj rule now.

qa.q: What did the caller say was inside the parcel?
qa.a: Drugs inside.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling when the phone dropped?
qa.a: Suraj felt shaken and frightened, hands trembling after breaking the pressure by hanging up.

qa.q: Which of Suraj's steps matter most, and why?
qa.a: Hanging up, checking the official number, telling a sister, and reporting to the bank and helpline within the hour, because speed limits harm.

qa.q: How might Suraj's sister have felt hearing everything?
qa.a: She was probably scared at first, then relieved and proud that Suraj told her straight away.

grounding: A young adult hangs up on a scam call, checks through the official number, tells a trusted person and reports quickly to the bank and helpline.

passage:
I sit across from Ira at the design studio, so I saw it happen. She had been on a call for twenty minutes, whispering, face grey. I heard "I'll pay now, sir" and saw her open the banking app.
Then she stopped. She stared at the screen for a long second, said, "I'm hanging up," and did. She walked straight to Zainab, our team lead, and said, "I think I'm being scammed. Can you sit with me?"
Zainab didn't ask why she'd stayed on so long. She opened the tax department's real website and read out the official helpline number. Ira called it: there was no case against her. Then, with Zainab beside her, she phoned her bank to freeze online payments and filed a report with the cyber-crime helpline before lunch.
I don't know what she felt afterwards. She laughed a bit shakily and ate her whole tiffin. That seemed like a good sign.

qa.q: Whose website did Zainab open?
qa.a: The tax department's real website.

qa.q: What might Ira have felt when she said 'I'm hanging up'?
qa.a: She likely felt frightened but suddenly clear, breaking the caller's pressure in one decisive moment.

qa.q: Which of Ira's actions gave her the best chance to limit harm?
qa.a: Hanging up, telling Zainab, checking the official helpline, freezing payments with the bank and reporting before lunch.

qa.q: How might Zainab have felt being asked to sit with Ira?
qa.a: Zainab probably felt concerned and trusted, glad Ira came to her without fear of blame.

grounding: A colleague watches a young woman hang up on a scam, check through the official number, tell a trusted person and report quickly.

passage:
Monday. Indu got a message: her electricity would be cut tonight unless she paid an "outstanding bill" through a link and called "the officer". He was polite but urgent. She paid ₹1,200 before she had finished thinking.
Tuesday. The officer called again: the payment had "failed technically", and she must pay ₹8,000 to reverse it. Indu felt the trap close. She said, "I'll call back," and hung up. Then she opened the electricity board's official app. Her bill showed zero dues.
Wednesday. At breakfast she told Afreen, her flatmate, everything, face burning. Afreen didn't laugh. "Let's do it together." They called the bank on the number on the back of Indu's card and blocked the card. They filed a complaint with the cyber-crime helpline, with screenshots.
Friday. The bank said part of the ₹1,200 might be traceable. Indu stuck a note on the fridge: Pause. Check the official app. Tell someone.

qa.q: What did the electricity board's official app show?
qa.a: Her bill showed zero dues.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling when she told Afreen at breakfast?
qa.a: She felt ashamed, face burning, but relieved to share it and not handle it alone.

qa.q: What did Indu do on Tuesday that turned things around?
qa.a: She hung up instead of paying more and checked her dues on the electricity board's official app.

qa.q: How might Afreen see Indu's story?
qa.a: Afreen sees it as something that could happen to anyone and feels protective, offering to act together.

grounding: Over a week a young woman stops paying, checks the official app, tells her flatmate and reports quickly to the bank and helpline.

passage: "Come, Lavanya, sit. You asked why I made you save the bank's number in your phone. Let me tell you about your cousin Nithya, last year, when she was twenty-four. A man called her saying he was from the bank. Her card would be blocked, he said, unless she shared the code that came by message. He was very polite, very urgent. She had already read out four digits when she stopped. Something in her said, why is the bank asking me? She cut the call. Then she did the clever thing: she opened the bank's own app and called the number printed there. They told her no one had called. She rang me next, crying, and I said, 'Report it now, don't wait.' So she called the bank to freeze the card and filed a report with the cybercrime helpline that same hour. Nothing was lost. That is why, kanna. Your Rukmini Paati is not just being fussy."

qa.q: How many digits had Nithya read out before she stopped?
qa.a: She had already read out four digits when she stopped.

qa.q: What was Nithya feeling when she rang Rukmini Paati?
qa.a: Nithya was shaken and frightened, crying after the near-miss, but also relieved that she had stopped in time.

qa.q: Which choice in the story was the turning point, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Nithya cutting the call and checking through the bank's own app and number broke the caller's urgency, and reporting it that same hour meant nothing was lost.

qa.q: How might Rukmini Paati have felt when Nithya called her crying?
qa.a: Rukmini Paati was probably frightened for Nithya but steady enough to tell her to report it at once, which is why she still tells the story.

grounding: Shows a victim stopping mid-scam, hanging up, checking through the official app and number, telling a trusted person and reporting quickly to the bank and cybercrime helpline.
